page.name: Immune Defense: From First Contact to Memory

props.markdown:
## 1. Crossing the boundary

Most infections begin when a bacterium, virus, fungus, or parasite reaches a body surface and bypasses a barrier. Skin blocks entry, while mucus in the nose and airways traps particles. Cilia move mucus toward the throat, and coughing or sneezing can remove it. Stomach acid and digestive enzymes damage many swallowed microbes. These defenses act before immune cells identify a particular species.

A cut, inhaled particle, contaminated food, or insect bite can create an opportunity for entry. Infection is more likely when the microbe reaches suitable tissue, avoids removal, and reproduces faster than early defenses can contain it.

## 2. Sensing danger

Cells in tissues recognize common molecular patterns found on microbes or released by damaged cells. They use pattern-recognition receptors, including receptors that detect some microbial proteins, sugars, or genetic material. Recognition does not require the body to have encountered that exact microbe before.

Nearby cells release chemical signals called cytokines and chemokines. These signals change local blood vessels and attract immune cells. The response is coordinated, but it is not perfectly specific: inflammation can also harm healthy tissue if it becomes excessive or prolonged.

## 3. Inflammation and containment

Inflamed blood vessels become more permeable, allowing fluid and defensive proteins to enter tissue. The area may become red, warm, swollen, and painful. Neutrophils often arrive early and engulf microbes. Macrophages can engulf microbes and debris, release signals, and help coordinate later responses.

Complement proteins in blood and tissues can coat microbes, attract immune cells, and damage certain microbial membranes. Together, these actions can slow spread and create time for adaptive immunity to develop.

A fever can make the body less favorable to some microbes and support immune activity, but a high or persistent fever can be dangerous. Symptoms reflect both the infection and the body’s response.

props.markdown:
## 1. From local alarm to targeted response

Some activated dendritic cells collect material from microbes and travel to nearby lymph nodes. There, they display small microbial fragments, called antigens, on surface molecules. This process helps connect the rapid innate response with adaptive immunity, which uses highly specific receptors on lymphocytes.

A lymphocyte responds only when its receptor and activation signals fit the presented antigen. This requirement helps reduce accidental activation. Lymphocytes then multiply, producing a larger population aimed at the same target.

## 2. B cells and antibodies

Activated B cells can become plasma cells, which release antibodies. Antibodies bind specific structures on an invader or its toxins. They may block a virus from attaching to cells, neutralize a toxin, mark a microbe for easier engulfment, or activate complement.

Antibodies work especially well against microbes and toxins outside cells. They are not a universal cure: viruses hiding inside cells and microbes protected within tissues also require cell-mediated responses. Antibody classes and their locations differ, but the central idea is selective binding followed by a useful defensive effect.

## 3. T cells and infected cells

Helper T cells release signals that activate and organize other immune cells. They can support B-cell responses and strengthen macrophage activity. Cytotoxic T cells recognize infected body cells displaying abnormal microbial fragments and can trigger those cells to die, limiting production of some intracellular pathogens.

Natural killer cells provide an additional early defense. They can detect certain stressed or abnormal cells, including some cells with reduced normal identification signals, and induce cell death. Their activity is part of innate immunity, although it complements later T-cell responses.

## 4. Balance matters

A strong response must be specific enough to control the microbe but regulated enough to limit collateral damage. Regulatory signals and the removal of activated cells help bring the response down after the threat declines. Vaccination uses this adaptive specificity without requiring the full disease.
props.title: Lesson

props.markdown:
## 1. Clearing the infection

An infection is controlled when microbes are destroyed, neutralized, or reduced below a level that causes continuing disease. Neutrophils, macrophages, antibodies, complement, and T cells may all contribute, depending on the pathogen and where it is located. Different microbes require different combinations of defenses.

Once danger signals fall, the body reduces inflammatory recruitment. Many short-lived immune cells die or are removed, while macrophages clear cellular debris. This change is not simply an “off switch”; specialized signals help shift tissue from active defense toward repair.

## 2. Tissue recovery

Repair depends on the site and severity of injury. Epithelial surfaces may replace damaged cells, while deeper wounds can form scar tissue. Fluid balance, pain, fatigue, and appetite may take time to normalize even after the microbe is gone. Lingering symptoms do not always mean that active infection continues, but worsening or severe symptoms need medical assessment.

The immune response itself can leave consequences. Excessive inflammation may damage organs, and some infections trigger symptoms after the original microbe has declined. Recovery therefore involves both pathogen control and limiting the body’s defensive collateral damage.

## 3. Building immune memory

After an adaptive response, some B and T cells become long-lived memory cells. Memory B cells can respond rapidly and generate antibodies after a later exposure. Memory T cells can recognize the relevant antigen and respond more efficiently. Antibody levels may decline over time, while memory can persist for varying periods.

Memory is specific and incomplete. A changed strain may partly escape earlier recognition, and protection differs by pathogen, person, vaccine, and time since exposure. Vaccines prepare adaptive memory without requiring a natural infection, though no vaccine guarantees perfect protection.

## 4. The airport-security analogy

Barriers resemble entrances and screening rules; innate immunity resembles rapid responders handling suspicious activity; adaptive immunity resembles specialists trained for a particular threat. Unlike an airport, the body must operate inside living tissue, so identification, removal, repair, and restraint happen together.

dashboards.name: 03 - Resolution, Recovery, and Memory

quickStart.keyIdea: Your immune system detects danger, slows an invader, recruits specialized defenses, remembers some threats, and repairs tissues during recovery.
quickStart.quickSummary:
An infection begins when a microbe crosses a barrier and starts multiplying. Fast innate defenses respond broadly through barriers, inflammation, cells, and proteins, buying time while the adaptive response develops.

Adaptive immunity targets specific features of the invader with antibodies and T cells. After the threat is controlled, inflammation resolves, damaged tissue repairs, and memory cells may improve protection against a later encounter.
